word:greek-nt:G0014.explanation: Agathoergeō means to do good or perform good deeds.

word:greek-nt:G0160.explanation: “Sudden” describes something that happens abruptly, without the gradual lead-up a person might expect. It can describe an event that arrives quickly and catches people unprepared. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears two times, in Luke 21:34 and 1 Thessalonians 5:3. Its central idea remains straightforward: the event comes unexpectedly and with little warning. The surrounding verse determines what specific event is being described.

word:greek-nt:G0256.explanation: Halphaios is a personal name, rendered Alphaeus.

word:greek-nt:G0371.explanation: “Unworthily” describes doing something in a way that does not properly match its worth or significance. It functions as an adverb, showing how an action is carried out rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 11:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to conduct that fails to give appropriate regard to what is being done.

word:greek-nt:G0528.explanation: Apantao means to go to meet, meet, or encounter.

word:greek-nt:G0573.explanation: Haplous means sound or good, and can also describe an eye as single.

word:greek-nt:G0630.explanation: Apolyo means to release, let go, or send away. It can also refer to divorcing a wife or sending a multitude away.

word:greek-nt:G0919.explanation: Bar-Jesus is a personal name for a sorcerer and false prophet at Paphos.

word:greek-nt:G0955.explanation: Belial is a proper name, preserved in English as “Belial,” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in 2 Corinthians 6:15. Since the word itself is presented as a name and no broader definition is supplied here, its precise significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage. The name should therefore be recognized as a distinct designation, not expanded into an unsupported list of meanings.

word:greek-nt:G0982.explanation: This word means “of this life,” describing something connected with life in the present world. It points to matters belonging to ordinary human existence, without by itself explaining whether those matters are good, bad, temporary, or lasting. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, so its meaning is focused and consistent rather than broadly varied across Scripture. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

word:greek-nt:G1013.explanation: Boulema means an intended purpose or plan. It can also mean a will.

word:greek-nt:G1048.explanation: Γάζαν names Gaza, an old town on the southern coast of Palestine.

word:greek-nt:G1251.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to give a hearing.” It describes the act of listening to someone or allowing that person to be heard, especially in the sense of granting attention to what is presented. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 23:35. Since no verse text is included here, the surrounding passage is needed to explain its precise force in that occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G1372.explanation: Dipsao means to be thirsty. It can also describe earnestly desiring something, as people may thirst for righteousness.

word:greek-nt:G1426.explanation: Dysphemia means an evil report or slander.

word:greek-nt:G1480.explanation: “Be accustomed” describes something familiar through regular practice or custom: a person is used to it rather than encountering it as something new. It expresses an established pattern of behavior or experience, not a single accidental act. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Luke 2:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic sense is familiarity formed by repeated practice or custom.

word:greek-nt:G1534.explanation: Eita means then, thereafter, or next, marking a fresh stage in what follows.

word:greek-nt:G1729.explanation: This word describes someone who is impoverished or needy—someone lacking the resources needed for ordinary support. It focuses on a person’s condition of need rather than naming a particular possession or circumstance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 4:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a person in poverty or serious material need.

word:greek-nt:G1765.explanation: This word means “to strengthen”—to make someone stronger, steadier, or better able to continue. It describes strengthening given to a person rather than merely describing strength as a quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing a focused use for the act of supplying strength or renewed ability. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:greek-nt:G1831.explanation: Exerchomai means to go out or come out.

word:greek-nt:G1927.explanation: This word means “to live as a visitor” or “to sojourn”—to stay in a place temporarily rather than belong there as a permanent resident. It describes a visitor or temporary resident. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts, so its basic sense is focused and consistent rather than broad or varied. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is simply on being present in a place or on living there temporarily.

word:greek-nt:G1952.explanation: Epileichō means to fail or fall short.

word:greek-nt:G1985.explanation: Episkopos means an overseer or supervisor. The overseer’s work includes shepherding the assembly.

word:greek-nt:G2135.explanation: Eunouchos means a eunuch, including a castrated person or one who voluntarily abstains from marriage. It can also refer to a high-ranking court official, as shown by the eunuch who had charge of a queen’s treasure.

word:greek-nt:G2438.explanation: Himas means a strap or thong. It can fasten a sandal, or it can be used to bind a person.

word:greek-nt:G2463.explanation: This word means “rainbow,” referring to the colored arc named in the text. It identifies something seen rather than an action, command, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, both in Revelation: Revelation 4:3 and Revelation 10:1. The same English rendering, “rainbow,” is used in each occurrence. Its basic meaning remains consistent, while the surrounding verse determines what the rainbow signifies in that particular passage.

word:greek-nt:G2661.explanation: Kataxioō means to deem or count worthy.

word:greek-nt:G2764.explanation: Keramikos means made of clay, or made by a potter.

word:greek-nt:G2900.explanation: This word means “mighty,” describing strength, power, or the ability to prevail. It is an adjective, so it identifies someone or something as possessing notable power rather than naming an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 5:6. The word’s central idea is strength that is substantial and effective. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its normal meaning points to what is powerful, strong, or able to accomplish much.

word:greek-nt:G3046.explanation: Litra means a Roman pound, a measure of about twelve ounces.

word:greek-nt:G3103.explanation: Methuselah is a personal name, referring to the man named Methuselah rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Luke’s recorded genealogy. As a proper name, its meaning is chiefly identification: it distinguishes this individual from the other people named in the genealogy. The word itself does not provide a broader description apart from the person it names.

word:greek-nt:G3158.explanation: Matthat is a personal name, referring to a man named Matthat. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, and both occurrences are in Luke chapter 3. The name appears in Luke 3:24 and Luke 3:29, identifying two people in the text’s recorded family line. Its meaning here is therefore primarily a person’s name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object.

word:greek-nt:G3194.explanation: Melite is a name for the island now called Malta.

word:greek-nt:G3312.explanation: Meristēs means a divider. It can also mean an arbiter.

word:greek-nt:G3367.explanation: Mēdeis means no one or nothing: it can forbid telling anyone and can describe expecting nothing in return.

word:greek-nt:G3389.explanation: This word means “matricide,” referring to one who kills a mother. It is a noun describing a person by that act. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 1:9. The word’s central meaning is specific and severe: it identifies someone who has killed his or her own mother, rather than describing a general kind of violence or wrongdoing. Its precise force in that verse is understood alongside the surrounding passage, but the word itself points directly to the killing of a mother.

word:greek-nt:G3420.explanation: This word means “remembrance”: keeping someone or something in mind so it is not forgotten. It is a noun describing the act or state of remembering, rather than an action performed by a person in the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Peter 1:15. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central meaning is remembrance or continued recollection.

word:greek-nt:G3486.explanation: Nahum is a personal name, rendered “Nahum.” In the Greek New Testament, it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This word occurs once, in Luke 3:25. The name itself gives the person’s designation, while the surrounding verse and genealogy provide the details of who he is in that passage. Its meaning here is therefore chiefly its function as a proper name: Nahum.

word:greek-nt:G3554.explanation: Nosos means disease, illness, or sickness.

word:greek-nt:G3598.explanation: Hodos means a way, a road, or a journey.

word:greek-nt:G3675.explanation: Homophrōn means like-minded, or of one mind.

word:greek-nt:G3716.explanation: Orthopodeō means to walk uprightly. It can also describe acting in line with what is true.

word:greek-nt:G3824.explanation: This word means “regeneration” or “renewal”: a bringing about of newness or restoration. It points to something being made new rather than merely continued in its former condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew and Titus, so its precise force in either passage comes from the surrounding words and subject. Its central idea remains a new beginning or renewed state. [p03:word:greek-nt:G3824:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G3824:occurrences]

word:greek-nt:G3921.explanation: This word describes entering or gaining access secretly, with the sense of infiltrating or slipping in unnoticed. It points to a quiet, concealed entrance rather than an open or clearly announced arrival. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Jude 1:4. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning is the act of secretly entering or insinuating oneself into a place or group.

word:greek-nt:G4120.explanation: Pleko means to weave, twist, or braid together.

word:greek-nt:G4186.explanation: Polytimos describes something of great value or very precious. It can also describe something costly, as with ointment.

word:greek-nt:G4216.explanation: This word describes something flooded or swept away by the powerful flow of a river. It presents water as a force carrying something along, emphasizing overwhelming movement rather than a gentle stream or ordinary wetness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 12:15. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: being carried away by a torrential flood.

word:greek-nt:G4339.explanation: Proselytos means a proselyte: a non-Jew who has been circumcised and adopted the Jews' religion.

word:greek-nt:G4375.explanation: Prosphiles means pleasing, acceptable, or lovely.

word:greek-nt:G4403.explanation: Prymna means the stern of a ship.

word:greek-nt:G4494.explanation: This word means “to be tossed about” or “to toss about.” It describes movement that is unsettled, shifting, or carried back and forth rather than remaining steady. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 1:6. The word’s central idea is instability expressed through tossing or being tossed, while the surrounding verse determines how that picture functions in context. It is a vivid term for something lacking firmness or being moved from one position to another.

word:greek-nt:G4546.explanation: Sampsōn is the name rendered Samson.

word:greek-nt:G4612.explanation: This word means “apron” or “aprons,” referring to a garment or covering worn over the front of the body. It names an ordinary physical item rather than an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 19:12. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the item is being described there.

word:greek-nt:G4667.explanation: Smyrna is the name of a great port in the Roman province of Asia.

word:greek-nt:G4689.explanation: Spendo means to pour out as a libation or drink offering.

word:greek-nt:G4825.explanation: Symboulos means an adviser or counselor.

word:greek-nt:G4869.explanation: Synaichmalōtos means a fellow captive or prisoner.

word:greek-nt:G4887.explanation: This word means “to be imprisoned with” or “to bind with.” It describes being joined to another person through shared bonds, including imprisonment. The emphasis is on being bound together rather than merely being near someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 13:3, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its meaning presents shared confinement or shared binding as the central idea.

word:greek-nt:G5008.explanation: This word refers to a girl, especially a little girl or young female child. It is a personal description rather than a title or abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 5:41. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning identifies a young girl. The two glosses, “girl” and “little girl,” express the same central idea with slightly different emphasis on youth or smallness.

word:greek-nt:G5101.explanation: Ti means who, which, what, or why.

word:greek-nt:G5219.explanation: Hypakouō means to listen, hearken, or obey. It may describe hearkening to a voice, or obedience to a command, even when winds and water are said to obey.

word:greek-nt:G5282.explanation: Hyponoeō means to suppose or think.

word:greek-nt:G5505.explanation: Chilias means a thousand, the number one thousand.

word:greek-nt:G6041.explanation: This word describes being earnest or envious—showing strong feeling toward something or someone. Its meaning can point to serious, wholehearted zeal, or to envy, depending on how the surrounding sentence uses it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 3:19. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the verse and passage context, which is not included here; its basic lexical sense is either earnest commitment or envious feeling.
